title: Primitive neighbours around every finite field
oneLine: An exact sieve and 53 explicit cycles close the finite remainder of the Sun–Hou ordering conjecture for every finite field with more than seven elements.
abstract: For every prime power q>7, the candidate supplies a circular ordering of all elements of Fq in which each adjacent sum is primitive. It inherits She’s large-field and prime-field ranges and treats the remaining 728 field orders: an exact sieved Chvátal–Erdős criterion covers 675, and explicit Hamilton cycles cover 53. The package records field moduli, exact witnesses, frozen cycles and non-destructive checks. A classical primitive-normal-basis Gray construction handles characteristic two; a sufficient deletion corollary follows from the same bound. This is a finite computer-assisted closure, not a new asymptotic theorem or a claim that every individual case was previously unknown.
keyResults: The primitive-sum graph on all of Fq is Hamiltonian for every prime power q>7, using inherited ranges and a finite closure.
Of 728 remaining orders, 675 satisfy the exact criterion and 53 have frozen explicit cycles.
A sufficient vertex-deletion bound follows from the same proof; over F32 it permits any six deletions.

narration:
Imagine arranging every number in a finite arithmetic system around a circle. There is one rule: add any two neighbours, and the answer must be a primitive element. A primitive element is a nonzero number whose successive powers visit every nonzero number in the system.

Sun and Hou asked whether such a circle always exists when the field has more than seven elements. Earlier work settled all sufficiently large fields, and all sufficiently large prime fields. This candidate closes the finite remainder.

There are seven hundred and twenty-eight field sizes to check. A mathematical bound settles six hundred and seventy-five. For the remaining fifty-three, the package gives actual circular orderings. A separate verifier checks that every field element appears exactly once and that every neighbouring sum has the required multiplicative order. It also checks the polynomial used to represent each field.

The smallest example on the page uses arithmetic modulo eleven. Its neighbouring sums are two, six, seven or eight: exactly the primitive elements in that field. This picture illustrates the rule; the downloadable certificates contain the full computational evidence.

The revised proof also gives a limited robustness result. Over the field with thirty-two elements, the bound still guarantees a circle after any six vertices are removed. This is a sufficient bound, not an optimal threshold.

The contribution needs perspective. Many small cases were already known, and the large-field theorem is inherited. This is a computer-assisted completion using established ideas. It remains an unrefereed candidate, without formal verification or independent external reproduction.

This is the Evidence Press briefing for the primitive-sum circle release, dated the twelfth of October, twenty twenty-six. The paper, code and certificates are linked on the page. This synthetic voice explanation is not additional evidence.
